notes.meaning: Hezekiah suffers from an illness so severe that no human doctor can cure it. The prophet Isaiah brings him a direct message from the Lord to settle the affairs of his family and kingdom, because his life is at an end. Such divine warnings often have unspoken conditions that leave room for prayer and repentance, as when Jonah warned Nineveh.

Unable to leave his bed to go to the temple or a private room, the king turns his face to the wall. This turns his attention away from the courtiers around his bed so he can speak directly to God without distraction. In his deep distress, his immediate reflex is to pour out his heart in prayer.

Hezekiah asks the Lord to remember his sincere, wholehearted obedience to God's law, and he weeps bitterly. Under the Old Testament covenant, God had promised long life to the faithful, so dying childless in his thirties felt like a sign of God's displeasure and threatened the future of David's royal line. He is not claiming God owes him anything as a debt, but he appeals to God's promises with honest tears.

Before Isaiah can even walk out of the central courtyard of the royal palace, God gives him a new word. The Lord identifies Himself as the God of David, showing He remembers His covenant promise to David's family. He assures Hezekiah that He has heard his prayer, seen his tears, and will heal him so completely that he will walk up to the temple to give thanks on the third day.

God promises to add fifteen years to Hezekiah's life and to protect Jerusalem from the king of Assyria. The Lord does this for the sake of His own honor and His covenant with David. The promise of personal healing served as a sure sign that the city would also be spared from its enemies.

differ.view: God did not change His eternal decree in response to Hezekiah, but had ordained from the start to grant these fifteen years through the king's prayers.

notes.meaning: Isaiah prescribes a paste of pressed figs to be placed directly on the king's infected boil, and Hezekiah begins to recover. While figs were a common ancient remedy used to draw out infection, the sudden recovery from a fatal illness was truly miraculous. God often chooses to work His supernatural healing through ordinary medical treatments rather than apart from them.

Hezekiah asks Isaiah for a miraculous sign to confirm the promise that he will be well enough to worship at the temple in three days. This request did not come from sinful doubt, but from a desire for assurance regarding such a great work of God. Unlike his ungodly father Ahaz, who had refused to ask for a sign, Hezekiah welcomes God's confirmation.

Isaiah offers the king a choice between having the sun's shadow advance ten steps or move backward ten steps. Hezekiah points out that shadows naturally lengthen as time passes, so moving forward would not be as obvious a miracle. He asks for the shadow to travel ten steps backward, which was entirely contrary to nature.

Isaiah calls on the Lord in prayer, and God brings the shadow back ten steps on the stairway or sundial of Ahaz. This great wonder proved God's power over the heavens and earth, showing Hezekiah that time itself was being extended for him. God graciously provided an undeniable sign to settle the king's faith.

The king of Babylon sends letters and a gift after learning of Hezekiah's sickness and recovery. While sent under the courteous banner of congratulating the king, the mission was also an effort to seek an alliance against their shared Assyrian foe and inquire about the miracle of the sun. The Babylonians worshipped heavenly bodies, so the sign on the dial caught their close attention.

Flattered by the attention of a foreign monarch, Hezekiah welcomes the envoys and gives them a complete tour of his palace, treasury, and military armory. Instead of telling them about the true God who healed him, he proudly shows off his own wealth and military power. This foolish display came from pride and an eagerness to impress a pagan nation.

Isaiah comes to Hezekiah with the authority of God's prophet to question him about his visitors and where they came from. Hezekiah admits with an air of satisfaction that they came from distant Babylon, and confesses that he hid nothing from them. He was blind to his own vanity, failing to realize that he had exposed his nation's riches to future conquerors.

Isaiah announces God's solemn judgment on the kingdom for its carnal pride and reliance on worldly strength. A day would come when all the wealth stored up by Judah's kings would be carried off into captivity by Babylon. Even worse, royal descendants of Hezekiah's own blood would be taken away to serve as court servants in the palace of the Babylonian king.

Hezekiah acknowledges that God's word through the prophet is just and good, submitting himself to the divine rebuke. He also finds mercy in the fact that God will grant peace and stability during the remainder of his own reign. True repentance leads a believer to accept God's discipline with humble patience.

differ.view: Some read Hezekiah's question as a selfish relief that avoids caring about the terrible hardships his descendants will face.

notes.meaning: The writer notes that the rest of Hezekiah's achievements, including his great engineering feat of carving a tunnel to bring fresh water into the city, are preserved in the royal records. This famous water project strengthened Jerusalem against sieges and provided for his people in times of peace. He used his royal power to leave behind lasting public benefits.

Hezekiah dies peacefully after his prolonged reign, and his son Manasseh succeeds him on the throne of Judah. Manasseh was born during the extra fifteen years God granted to Hezekiah, yet he went on to lead Judah into terrible wickedness. Godly parents cannot pass down faith by blood alone, for each generation must choose to obey the Lord for itself.
